title: How to Stop Likes, Ums, and Other Distracting Speaking Behaviors
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart treats filler words, mispronunciations, verbalized panic and fidgeting as Poise problems within Erik Palmer's PVLEGS framework for speech delivery, and lays out a five-step habit-change protocol for eliminating them. The distinctive move is that the teacher runs the protocol on himself first, using his own tics as the worked example, on the grounds that self-experimentation both establishes credibility with students and tests whether the method works. The steps are to identify the behavior that must die, build an external reminder of it, correct it on the spot whenever it surfaces, recruit someone to give regular feedback, and change tactics if months pass without improvement. He suggests a first lesson in which students watch film of themselves speaking and choose their own target behavior, with a low-tech version using a class video uploaded as link-only and a computer lab session. The underlying principle he names is making the unconscious conscious. The piece ends by conceding that habit change is hard and inviting readers to abandon a method that is not working rather than abandon the goal.
points: Stuart locates filler words and fidgeting inside Palmer's PVLEGS delivery framework, so they become a named instructional target rather than a vague annoyance.
The protocol requires the teacher to fix his own tics first, which he defends as both a credibility move with students and an honest test of whether the method works.
Film is the diagnostic instrument: monthly recordings of your own instruction reviewed while doing something mindless, or a class video students review to pick their own must-die behavior.
In-the-moment correction is deliberately gentle, restating the sentence or putting down the coffee cup rather than any form of self-punishment.
Feedback is delegated and divided, with a named observant student watching for one tic on a set day and a spouse or colleague watching for another.
quotes: Part of quality speaking instruction — particularly speech delivery instruction — is helping students eliminate their distracting speech behaviors. If you're familiar with Erik Palmer's PVLEGS acronym for speech delivery (a must-use, in my opinion), such behaviors are Poise issues.

First, I think we have to self-experiment: how do we get rid of our own distracting tics? In the below process, I use myself as an example. Self-experimentation makes us more credible for our students and also helps us see whether something can really work or not.
What you're trying to do here is make the unconscious conscious. Had I known how absurdly distracting my toying with a paperclip was in this clip, I wouldn't have done it.

So for example, with the “fer” thing, I'm going to tell one of my more observant third hour kids to keep an eye out for it on Wednesdays. For “like,” that's something both my wife, Crystal, and I struggle with, so we're going to make a blood pact not to allow another “like” to pass from the other's lips without dire punishment (and/or gentle reminding).
Habit change is challenging, but not impossible. If you find yourself not improving after a few months of this, try something new.
